Eggs of the Tongue sole (Cynoglossus macrolepidotus) are demersal and adhesive, with the chorion measuring approximately 0.44 mm in diameter. From this egg diameter, the calculated wet weight at birth is estimated to be 0.000045 g [Wwb = 0.000045 g], a minute mass that implies a substantial relative growth requirement to attain the juvenile stage. Embryonic development proceeds rapidly at the prevailing water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], with hatching occurring after just 1.5 days [ab = 1.5 days]. This brief incubation period is typical of many tropical flatfishes, where elevated thermal conditions accelerate developmental rates. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on its endogenous reserves, and the transition to first exogenous feeding must occur quickly to prevent starvation-related mortality. The timing of this critical trophic switch is therefore a key determinant of early survival and subsequent recruitment success.

Field surveys indicate that sexual maturation in C. macrolepidotus is closely tied to body size rather than age alone. The onset of puberty, marked by the commencement of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis, occurs when individuals attain a total length of 19.1 cm [Lp = 19.1 cm]. Concomitantly, the wet weight at puberty is recorded at 36.6 g [Wwp = 36.6 g], reflecting the somatic growth necessary to support reproductive function. This size threshold is comparable to that observed in other cynoglossid flatfishes from similar subtropical habitats. Achieving this developmental milestone typically requires a sustained feeding regime, as the species forages on benthic invertebrates. The energetic demands of reaching this point are substantial, and individuals that fail to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves may delay maturation until the following season.

The maximum recorded body size for sexually mature adults of Tongue sole, based on extensive trawl surveys, reaches an ultimate total length of 39.1 cm [Li = 39.1 cm]. Correspondingly, the ultimate female wet weight is estimated at 340 g [Wwi = 340 g], derived from allometric growth equations applied to field-collected specimens. This asymptotic size represents the culmination of several years of somatic growth, after which energy is increasingly diverted toward reproductive output. The length-weight relationship in this species is positively allometric, indicating that larger females are disproportionately heavier and likely capable of producing larger clutches. Mature females are iteroparous, spawning multiple times over their lifespan, and the onset of reproductive senescence, if it occurs, has not been well documented in wild populations.

Longevity records for C. macrolepidotus, obtained from annual growth increment analysis of sagittal otoliths, indicate that individuals can survive for a maximum lifespan of 6 years [am = 6 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This estimate was derived from captive-rearing studies conducted at a constant water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], which closely matches the thermal regime of their native coastal habitat. This lifespan is moderate among flatfishes, being shorter than that of larger, deeper-dwelling species but longer than that of many small-bodied, fast-maturing tropical fishes. Growth rates are most rapid during the first two years of life, after which the annual increment declines noticeably. The combination of a relatively brief lifespan and early maturation suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward rapid turnover and high annual reproductive effort.

A comparative analysis of reproductive biology within the family Cynoglossidae reveals that Tongue sole exhibits a moderate fecundity relative to its body size. Documented spawning events occur during the warmer months, when water temperatures exceed the species' thermal minimum for gonadal development. Females below the size threshold at puberty of 19.1 cm [Lp = 19.1 cm] are rarely observed in a gravid state, confirming the tight linkage between size and functional maturity observed in related species. The corresponding wet weight of 36.6 g [Wwp = 36.6 g] marks the point at which sufficient energy reserves are available to support the production of a first clutch. Future studies would benefit from quantifying the relationship between maternal size and fecundity across the species' geographic range to better understand how environmental gradients shape life-history variation in this commercially important flatfish.
